title: Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah chairs 31st meeting of the Southern Zonal Council in Mahabalipuram, Tamil Nadu
subtitle:

body_text:
Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah chaired the 31 st meeting of the Southern Zonal Council in Mahabalipuram, Tamil Nadu. The meeting was attended by Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Shri C. Joseph Vijay, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Shri Chandrababu Naidu, Karnataka Chief Minister Shri D. K. Shivakumar, Keralam Chief Minister Shri V. D. Satheesan, Puducherry Lieutenant Governor Shri K. Kailashnathan, Andaman and Nicobar Islands Lieutenant Governor Admiral (Retd.) D. K. Joshi Lakshadweep Administrator Shri Praful Patel, and the Deputy Chief Minister of Telangana Shri Bhatti Vikramarka Mallu. Chief Secretaries, Advisors and other senior officers of the state governments, as well as senior officers of the Central Government, also attended the meeting.
Addressing the meeting, Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah said that this region of South India is a very important region for the development of the country. He said that whether it is literature, Research and Development (R&D), space, IT, AI, industrial development or agriculture, South India has always contributed in every sector. South India has played a very major role in all areas of the country’s IT, automobiles, pharmaceuticals and infrastructure development, and that is why a large amount of foreign direct investment has also come to the South.
Shri Amit Shah said that the entire development journey of South India has been based on three pillars — high literacy rate, trained manpower and technical expertise in the utilisation of deep seas. These three pillars have made South India the biggest contributor to the country’s development. The people of South India and the governments have also established many excellent traditions in the fields of innovation and revenue generation. He said that the whole of India should learn from South India in these two areas.
Union Home Minister said that on the occasion of the 80 th Independence Day, Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi has stated that what has not been achieved in the last seven decades, we must accomplish in the next five to seven years; only then will we be able to secure our place in the global competition. To achieve such development, every state will have to contribute to it.
Shri Amit Shah said that since 2014, efforts have been made to transform the Zonal Council into a meaningful platform. The Zonal Council is essentially a constitutional mechanism that, over a long period, had gradually been reduced to a mere formality. Comparing the periods of 2004-2014 and 2014-2026, he said that while the Council previously held an average of two and a half meetings annually, it now holds six meetings each year. He mentioned that a total of 70 Zonal Council meetings have taken place since 2014, during which 1,445 out of 1,869 issues, approximately 80%, were resolved. Shri Shah added that many issues pending for 60 years have been settled through these Zonal Council meetings.
Union Home Minister said that in North India five out of the eight issues related to sharing of river waters had been persisting since the pre-British era. A final agreement was reached five months ago, and by resolving 100% of the issues, spanning from Kashmir to Uttar Pradesh, a dispute-free North India has been achieved.
Shri Amit Shah said that the southern states are the main pillars of the country’s progress, and the progress of the southern states depends on water. Whether it is agriculture, industry, healthy citizens or the environment, water is the soul of this region in all these four areas.
Shri Amit Shah observed that protecting the interests of one's state is not wrong; however, if the process of protecting interests results in states being deprived of water for years while it simply flows into the sea, then no actual interest is being served. He said that linking major rivers, from the Brahmaputra to the Kaveri and Godavari, could ensure that India faces no water shortage for the next 100 years. This initiative could also facilitate the creation of multiple waterways, which would not only save fuel and improve the environment but also provide a cost-effective transportation system.
Union Home Minister Shri Amit Shah emphasized the need for the early resolution of pending water-related issues concerning southern states through joint meetings involving the Ministry of Jal Shakti, the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Inter-State Council, and the respective states. The southern states agreed with the Home Minister's suggestion to resolve these pending water disputes expeditiously through mutual dialogue and constructive solutions. Regarding issues concerning the division of assets and liabilities between Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, both states agreed to resolve these matters in consultation with the Ministry of Home Affairs.
Shri Amit Shah said that the swift investigation of cases of rape against women and children, and the early disposal of rape and POCSO cases through the implementation of Fast Track Special Courts (FTSC) are very sensitive issues. He said that these issues need to be viewed with great sensitivity at the level of the Chief Ministers. The Home Minister said that after the introduction of the new criminal laws, many tools have become available to us for accelerating the entire process.
Home Minister said that malnutrition, stunting and the school dropout ratio are very important for our future generations. We should not be satisfied with anything less than 100 per cent in addressing the school dropout ratio. Shri Shah said that currently the school dropout ratio for the entire country stands at 9.5, and if all states make even incremental improvements, we can bring it down below 3 per cent. He said that if the national dropout ratio goes below 3 per cent, children will become educated citizens and a conducive environment will be created in the country for implementing the spirit of the Constitution in its true sense down to the grassroots.
Union Home Minister said that we must also pay special attention to malnutrition. In a way, nutrition schemes are also linked to the school dropout ratio. He further said that we are moving towards an even more dangerous problem of stunting, that is, stunted growth. This appears to be gradually becoming a national problem that can impair the capabilities of our future generations. Therefore, we must take malnutrition and stunting very seriously. Shri Shah said that the fight against malnutrition was initiated by Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh, which was eventually accepted across the country. Now there is a need to pay special attention to it. After 80 years of independence, we cannot place the burden of malnourished children on this country. If implementation is carried out with sensitivity at the Chief Minister level on this issue, the country can be freed from this problem. He said that it is the responsibility of all of us to contribute towards building an educated and healthy India.
Shri Amit Shah said that today a drug-free India is a necessity for every government and our society. The Ministry of Home Affairs of the Government of India has prepared a three-year roadmap in which the roles of several departments of the states and the Centre have been defined. Until all departments of the Central Government and all departments of all state governments join this movement, we will not be able to save the coming generation from this evil. He said that it is the responsibility of us all to contribute towards building an educated and healthy India.
***

enrichment.summary: Union Home Minister Amit Shah chaired the 31st Southern Zonal Council meeting in Mahabalipuram, Tamil Nadu, attended by chief ministers/administrators of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Puducherry, Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshadweep and Telangana. He said 70 Zonal Council meetings since 2014 have resolved about 80% (1,445 of 1,869) of pending issues, cited resolution of North India's river-water disputes as a model, and urged southern states to resolve pending water disputes and the Andhra Pradesh-Telangana asset/liability division through dialogue with the Centre. He also raised interlinking of rivers, Fast Track Special Courts for POCSO cases, reducing school dropout ratio below 3%, tackling malnutrition/stunting, and a three-year roadmap for a drug-free India.
enrichment.context:
Zonal Councils are statutory (not constitutional, despite the release calling them a 'constitutional mechanism') bodies set up under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 to foster cooperative federalism and resolve inter-state disputes on issues like water, boundaries, and economic planning. There are five Zonal Councils (Northern, Southern, Eastern, Western, Central) plus the North Eastern Council, each chaired by the Union Home Minister with state chief ministers as members. These platforms have historically met infrequently and been criticised as ineffective talking shops, so the claimed increase in meeting frequency and issue-resolution rate is presented as an achievement of the current government's federalism push.

Inter-state river water disputes are a recurring flashpoint in Indian federalism, governed by Article 262 and the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, with tribunals like the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal having long adjudicated disputes among southern states (Cauvery among Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Puducherry; Krishna-Godavari among Telangana and Andhra Pradesh). The Andhra Pradesh-Telangana asset and liability division stems from the 2014 bifurcation under the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, aspects of which (including river water sharing and asset division) remain unresolved. The idea of interlinking rivers via a National Perspective Plan (originating from the National Water Development Agency) has long been debated for its potential to address water scarcity and enable inland waterways, but faces environmental, cost, and inter-state consent challenges.

prelims_questions.question: The Zonal Councils in India were established under which of the following?
prelims_questions.explanation: Zonal Councils are statutory bodies created under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, not constitutional bodies, to promote cooperative federalism among grouped states.

prelims_questions.question: Inter-state river water disputes in India are primarily adjudicated under which legislative framework?
options: The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956
The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
prelims_questions.explanation: The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, enacted under Article 262 of the Constitution, provides the mechanism for adjudication of water disputes between states, typically through tribunals.

mains_questions.question: Zonal Councils were envisaged as instruments of cooperative federalism but have often functioned as mere advisory bodies. Discuss their utility in resolving inter-state disputes with reference to recent claims of increased effectiveness.
Examine the challenges in resolving inter-state river water sharing disputes in India and evaluate the feasibility of the river-interlinking programme as a long-term solution.

study_notes.reason: The release provides testable factual core about Zonal Councils (statutory basis, composition, structure) while also offering substantial material on cooperative federalism, inter-state water disputes, and river-linking policy debates for Mains analysis.

prelims.point: Zonal Councils are statutory bodies established under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 — not constitutional bodies, despite common misstatement.
prelims.why_important: A classic UPSC distinction-trap: testing whether aspirants know Zonal Councils are statutory, not constitutional, unlike bodies such as the Finance Commission.

prelims.point: There are five Zonal Councils (Northern, Southern, Eastern, Western, Central) plus the North Eastern Council, each chaired by the Union Home Minister.
prelims.why_important: Composition and chairmanship of Zonal Councils is a recurring factual point tested via statement-based questions.

prelims.point: The Southern Zonal Council comprises Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Puducherry, Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshadweep and Telangana.
prelims.why_important: Membership composition of specific zonal councils can appear in matching-type prelims questions.

prelims.point: Inter-state river water disputes are governed by Article 262 and adjudicated under the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, with tribunals like the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal.
prelims.why_important: Article 262 and the associated tribunal mechanism is a frequently tested constitutional-legal provision on federal water disputes.

prelims.point: The Andhra Pradesh-Telangana asset and liability division arises from the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014, following the state's bifurcation.
prelims.why_important: Links a current governance issue to its originating legislation, a common prelims linkage format.

prelims.point: River interlinking proposals stem from the National Perspective Plan formulated by the National Water Development Agency.
prelims.why_important: Tests knowledge of the institutional origin of the interlinking of rivers scheme, often confused with other water bodies.

mains.point: Government claims Zonal Councils have been revitalised since 2014, citing increased meeting frequency (2.5/year to 6/year) and an 80% issue-resolution rate, positioning this as a cooperative federalism achievement.
mains.analytical_use: Useful for questions on strengthening inter-state coordination bodies and evaluating the effectiveness of statutory federal mechanisms like Zonal Councils.

mains.point: Persistent inter-state river water disputes among southern states (e.g., Cauvery, Krishna-Godavari) illustrate the tension between protecting state interests and national/regional water security.
mains.analytical_use: Deployable in questions on causes and resolution mechanisms for inter-state water conflicts and the balance between state autonomy and cooperative federalism.

mains.point: River interlinking (Brahmaputra to Kaveri and Godavari) is proposed as a solution to water scarcity and could also enable inland waterway transport, though it carries environmental, cost and inter-state consent challenges.
mains.analytical_use: Core material for 'Discuss the feasibility and challenges of river interlinking in India' type questions covering environmental, economic and federal dimensions.

mains.point: Unresolved Andhra Pradesh-Telangana asset/liability division nearly a decade after bifurcation highlights implementation gaps in post-reorganisation settlements.
mains.analytical_use: Can support answers on challenges in implementing state bifurcation agreements and the role of the Centre as mediator.

mains.point: High school dropout ratio (9.5% nationally) and rising child stunting are flagged as governance priorities linked to human capital and constitutional goals.
mains.theme: Human development and social sector governance
mains.analytical_use: Relevant for questions on addressing malnutrition and education outcomes through inter-governmental coordination.

mains.point: Fast Track Special Courts for POCSO cases and a three-year roadmap for a drug-free India reflect Centre-state coordination on criminal justice and social welfare.
mains.theme: Criminal justice reform and social welfare coordination
mains.analytical_use: Supports answers on implementation challenges of victim-centric justice mechanisms and coordinated drug-control policy.
